chunks: My father (RA) said: Sa'd ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya ibn 'Imran al-Halabi, from Ma'la Abu 'Uthman, from 'Ali ibn Hanzalah, from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS) that he said:

The privileged one is led along the path of the adverse until the people say: 'He is so similar to them that he must be one of them.' Then privilege reaches him. And sometimes the adverse one is led along the path of the privileged until the people say: 'He is so similar to them that he must be one of them.' Then adversity reaches him. Verily, whoever Allah, the Exalted, knows to be privileged, even if the only time that remains in the world is the hiccup of a she-camel, He will bring his life to an end with privilege.

key_terms.السَّعِيدُ: The privileged one / The happy one (destined for success)
key_terms.الْأَشْقِيَاءُ: The adverse ones / The miserable ones (destined for failure)
key_terms.خُتِمَ لَهُ: He was sealed / His end was brought about
key_terms.فَوَاقَ نَاقَةٍ: The hiccup of a she-camel (a brief moment of time)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between apparent status and ultimate destiny in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid* elucidates the distinction between apparent worldly status and ultimate divine decree, illustrating how the 'Saeed' (happy) may be mistaken for the 'Ashiq' (miserable) and vice versa due to external circumstances. It emphasizes that Allah’s knowledge is the definitive guarantee of one’s final state, whether one ends with happiness or misery, regardless of the brevity of remaining time. This concept reinforces the Shia understanding of *al-Hikmah* (divine wisdom) in testing believers through apparent contradictions between their inner destiny and outer reality.
